prompt: How many Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes does the language L of binary strings ending in 01 have?

options.explanation: Two classes would only distinguish "ends in 01" from the rest, but "ends in 0" and "ends in 1 (not 01)" have different futures: the suffix `1` accepts the first only.
One for each two-bit ending (00, 01, 10, 11) overcounts. Endings 00 and 10 behave identically: what matters is just "the last symbol was 0".
Correct: "ends in 01", "ends in 0", and everything else (ε or ends in 1 but not 01). So the minimal DFA has 3 states.

options.text: Infinitely many, since L is infinite
options.explanation: An infinite language can have finitely many classes; that is exactly what regular means.

workedExample:
Group strings by what suffixes they need:

| Class | Example | Suffix 1? | Suffix ε? |
|---|---|---|---|
| ends 01 | `01` | no | yes |
| ends 0 | `10` | yes | no |
| other | `11`, ε | no | no |

The three rows differ in some column, so the classes are distinct. These classes also form a closed transition system: on 0 every class goes to ends-0; on 1 ends-0 goes to ends-01 and the other classes go to other. Only ends-01 accepts, so all strings within each class have identical futures. There are exactly 3, and the minimal DFA has 3 states.

prompt: Which are valid Myhill–Nerode arguments that a language is not regular? Select all that apply.

options.text: For palindromes, prefixes of any number of a’s then b are separated by appending the first prefix’s number of a’s
options.explanation: Valid. Append as many a’s as occur before the b in the first prefix. It becomes a palindrome; a prefix with any different number of a’s does not.

options.text: For a’s followed by equally many b’s, different lengths of initial a-runs are separated by a matching number of b’s
options.explanation: Valid. A suffix of i b’s completes a prefix of i a’s into the language but rejects any prefix with a different number of a’s.

options.text: a*b* has infinitely many a-prefixes, so it is not regular
options.explanation: Invalid. All a-only prefixes have the same allowed continuations in this language. Infinitely many prefixes do not help unless they are pairwise distinguishable.

options.text: Even-length strings: ε, a, aa, aaa, ... are infinitely many strings, so not regular
options.explanation: Invalid. Only 2 classes exist (even or odd so far). For example ε and aa are equivalent.

workedExample: You need infinitely many prefixes that can be distinguished pairwise, not merely infinitely many strings. For palindromes, take different a-runs followed by b; an a-run matching the first prefix completes only that palindrome. For equal a-then-b counts, a matching b-run separates different initial a-runs. In `a*b*`, however, all a-only prefixes have the same future possibilities. In even-length strings only parity matters, so infinitely many prefixes still fall into two classes.
